extracted.intended_audience: English-speaking travelers and expatriates in Paris (early 20th-century general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical principles for low-cost, hospitable home entertaining and for exploring Paris on evening walks (timing, attitude, and suggested routes). Drawn from a travel-memoir style chapter with actionable recommendations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcome guests and serve what you serve yourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: "Guests are _always_ welcome, and we never feed them better than we feed ourselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company is the rule, not the exception. Keep hospitality inclusive and simple: serve the same food you would for yourselves rather than staging special extravagant meals for guests. This preserves warm conviviality without financial strain or pretense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make entertaining a burden or a great expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertaining should not be a burden or a great expense; avoid splurging or offering meals beyond your income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues against competing with wealthier hosts or restaurants and advises against wearing oneself out to impress guests. Occasional splurges are acceptable, but regular entertaining should stay within means to avoid discomfort and pretense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise cleanliness and the quality/quantity of food over perfect housekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am finicky only about cleanliness and the quality and quantity of food. The rest doesn't matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housekeeping need not be rigidly scheduled or obsessive; focus on clean surroundings and decent, sufficient food. Ignore minor disorder (wash days, spring-cleaning timing, etc.) when it conflicts with hospitality and life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, pragmatic provisioning for unexpected guests
rubrics_metrics.description: When extra guests arrive, add an extra plate and get a little more of what you're having; in a big city getting more food quickly is no problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics: keep nearby shops in mind (bakery, épicerie, Sempé for eggs) so you can supplement meals at short notice. This enables spontaneous hospitality without elaborate planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain regular low-cost 'at-home' receiving days
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold a weekly receiving afternoon (author's example: Wednesdays) as an informal low-cost way to see friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A regular 'at home' creates community and social contact without extravagant entertaining. It's acceptable if crowded; simple refreshments and conviviality are the point rather than formal presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be spontaneous and inclusive in invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue inclusive, spontaneous invitations (e.g., 'if there is a Mrs. K bring her with you') to encourage attendance and serendipitous connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spontaneity can bring remarkable contacts and opportunities (the lawyer who suggested the author's research direction is an example). Inclusive invitations lower social friction and broaden networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use informal home gatherings to foster intellectual and professional exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Table-talk and after-dinner conversation can lead to new ideas, collaborations, and professional advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author attributes major scholarly directions and books to conversations with dinner guests; thus, host regular informal gatherings to stimulate discussion and opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide charity and hospitality to those in need
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to evident need (feed the hungry, give clothing) when one can—small acts of charity are part of hospitable living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: feeding Mr. Thompson and giving him an overcoat despite limited means. Practical charity is framed as moral and humane even when resources are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan evening walks around museum/library closing times (five to seven in winter)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you want to follow me in Paris walks through this chapter, plan your strolls from five to seven during the winter months."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends walking at nightfall—after libraries and museums close—to combine exercise with exploration. Timing should adjust by season (closing hours vary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve daytime for churches, museums, and palaces; use evenings for street exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: "Use your precious days for churches and museums and palaces. After they are closed, walk for an hour or two each night."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make efficient use of limited tourist/residency time: see interiors and formal sites by day, and use evenings for discovery of neighborhoods, people, and atmospheric detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be catholic in tastes; combine multiple interests on walks
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt broad tastes—architecture, history, literature, human observation—and be willing to jump from one interest to another during walks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a specific goal (walls, mediaeval traces, famous names) but be ready to switch between architecture, history, and observing people; this diversity yields richer impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look actively—'look before you see'; effort yields deeper impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Seek and ye shall find' is a promise with a condition attached to it. You have to look before you see. An effort of the will is required."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active observation and focused attention are essential; casual viewing yields false or shallow impressions. The anecdote about using opera glasses to see Messina's damage underscores deliberate looking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry a map and know arrondissement divisions to plan routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing arrondissements and carrying a map helps plan nightfall walks and understand the city's layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the author prefers accidental discovery, practical knowledge of arrondissement boundaries and a map help you design widening-circle walks and avoid getting lost between inner and outer quarters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer discovery over guide-books (but use suggested strolls if needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have a horror of guide-books... I love to find my way without pre-meditation and by accident. But many readers will never have the same opportunity... Why should I resist the temptation of indicating some of the strolls..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While serendipity is prized, the author concedes that some readers need concrete routes; thus, avoid slavish reliance on guides but accept that suggested walks can be helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested nightfall routes and notable spots to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Author recommends specific night-walk routes and highlights: Rue de Rivoli → Rue Saint-Antoine → Bastille; Rue du Temple, Rue des Rosiers, Place des Vosges, Pont Sully, Ile Saint-Louis, Notre Dame; Second Arrondissement routes from Place des Victoires to Grands Boulevards; Rue du Faubourg du Temple → Rue de Belleville → Eglise Saint-Jean-Baptiste → Ménilmontant → Buttes-Chaumont; Quai de Jemmapes; Montmartre steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete route suggestions serve as starting points for nightfall exploration; they illustrate variety (Ghetto streets, islands, working-class quarters, hilltop views) and can be adapted by season and interest.
